contraindications: Valproate: hyperammonemia (urea cycle inhibition) and hepatotoxicity; avoid in cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy.
interactions: Levetiracetam: renally cleared, no hepatic metabolism and no interaction with lactulose, rifaximin or lisinopril; dose by creatinine clearance.
Lorazepam: glucuronidated without active metabolites, preferred over diazepam or midazolam in cirrhosis for seizure termination; sedation adds to hepatic encephalopathy.
Lactulose and rifaximin with levetiracetam, lorazepam or lisinopril: no clinically relevant interaction.
output.proposed: Antiseizure drug selection in cirrhosis: levetiracetam, lorazepam, valproate, phenytoin, lacosamide; with lactulose, rifaximin and lisinopril
output.summary: Levetiracetam (renally cleared) and lorazepam (glucuronidated) suit cirrhosis. Avoid valproate (hyperammonemia, hepatotoxicity). Phenytoin needs free levels with low albumin; lacosamide needs hepatic dose reduction. No interaction with lactulose, rifaximin or lisinopril.
warnings: Phenytoin and fosphenytoin: hepatic metabolism and high protein binding; with albumin 2.4 g/dL total levels underestimate free drug; measure free levels if used.
Lacosamide: reduce the dose in mild to moderate hepatic impairment (maximum 300 mg per day); not recommended in severe impairment.
Phenobarbital and carbamazepine: enzyme induction, sedation and hepatic metabolism; avoid where alternatives exist.

action_criteria.rationale: Second-line drugs for status epilepticus differ in hepatic metabolism and ammonia effects, which changes the choice in Child-Pugh C cirrhosis.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not withhold a benzodiazepine for seizure termination because of hepatic encephalopathy (lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV, up to 4 mg per dose; AES 2016); avoid benzodiazepines for agitation or sedation.
Do not prescribe sedating opioids, which precipitate and prolong HE; for pain use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day.
Do not use valproate: it causes hyperammonemia and hepatotoxicity in cirrhosis.
Do not use scheduled benzodiazepines as maintenance antiseizure therapy; maintain with levetiracetam.
required_recommendations: Terminate NCSE: lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (up to 4 mg per dose), repeated once if needed, then IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (maximum 4500 mg) as the second-line drug, with EEG-guided escalation in the ICU if it persists (AES 2016).

Admit to the ICU with airway protection: GCS 9 and SpO2 92% after a seizure; give oxygen, aspiration precautions, and intubate if he cannot protect his airway or anaesthetic treatment is needed, without waiting for a GCS below 8.
Resume levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily (dose for renal function) with an adherence plan supervised by his girlfriend.
Give parenteral thiamine before any glucose.

Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours by nasogastric tube while he cannot swallow safely, until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury. Continue rifaximin 550 mg twice daily.
Identify and treat the precipitants of HE: the seizures, missed levetiracetam and possible infection (screen cultures); replace potassium to 4.0 mmol/L or more.
Refer for liver transplant assessment once recovered: decompensated cirrhosis with recurrent overt HE, Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 23, abstinent for a year (EASL 2018).

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

accepted: Non-convulsive status epilepticus following breakthrough generalized tonic-clonic seizure (subtherapeutic levetiracetam 8 µg/mL) with concurrent overt hepatic encephalopathy in alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 23); both lower consciousness to GCS 9.

differential.diagnosis: Severe hepatic encephalopathy (sole cause of GCS 9)
differential.key_features: Cirrhosis, prior HE episodes and 2-3 days of increasing confusion support concurrent HE, but the continuous spike-and-wave on EEG shows that HE is not the sole cause of the coma.
The EEG shows ongoing ictal activity rather than post-ictal slowing.

differential.diagnosis: Anoxic brain injury from prolonged seizure
differential.key_features: Brief convulsion, SpO2 92% without documented prolonged hypoxia; NCSE explains the EEG.
Sober for a year, no ophthalmoparesis or nystagmus; give thiamine before glucose regardless.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade, evidence of liver disease and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).

Child-Pugh C (11 to 12: bilirubin 3.6 3, albumin 2.4 3, INR 2.0 2, no ascites 1, HE 2 or 3 points, since the HE grade cannot be assigned during NCSE); MELD-Na 23 (creatinine 1.2, bilirubin 3.6, INR 2.0, sodium 134).
Persistent unresponsiveness after a witnessed seizure requires an EEG to exclude NCSE: clinical examination cannot distinguish severe HE from NCSE.
Cirrhotic patients on antiseizure drugs need adherence and level monitoring; subtherapeutic levels are a common breakthrough trigger.

Levetiracetam (renally cleared) is the antiseizure drug of choice in cirrhosis; lacosamide needs dose reduction in hepatic impairment; valproate (hyperammonemia, hepatotoxicity) and enzyme inducers are avoided.

The admission bloods were drawn within about an hour of the convulsion: lactate rises immediately after a generalized seizure, whereas CK rises over hours and peaks 24-72 hours later, so a normal early CK does not argue against the seizure (Brigo 2015).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Post-ictal states typically resolve within 30-60 minutes; persistent unresponsiveness requires an EEG to exclude NCSE.
red_herrings.data_point: Known seizure disorder on levetiracetam — assume post-ictal
red_herrings.intended_effect: Wait for the post-ictal state to resolve without an EEG.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Severe HE and NCSE are clinically indistinguishable and can coexist; an EEG is mandatory.
red_herrings.data_point: Ammonia 108 with cirrhosis — assume HE alone
red_herrings.intended_effect: Treat only HE without an EEG.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: NCSE (continuous spike-and-wave on EEG) superimposed on overt HE, both causing GCS 9; subtherapeutic levetiracetam from missed doses; the EEG is the critical test that separates NCSE from a post-ictal state or HE alone; valproate is avoided in cirrhosis.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 4 required actions (core labs with levetiracetam level, CT, EEG, antiseizure drug check) + recommended infection screen; two simultaneous diagnoses (NCSE + HE) both lowering consciousness; antiseizure drug choice constrained by cirrhosis.

past_medical_history: Alcohol-related cirrhosis with two prior HE episodes

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. F. is a 44-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis, prior seizure disorder treated with levetiracetam, and an established HE prophylaxis regimen, who was brought by ambulance in an unresponsive state. His girlfriend witnessed him having a generalized tonic-clonic seizure approximately 30 minutes before EMS arrival. He had been increasingly confused over the prior 2-3 days — she attributed it to usual HE episodes which he has had twice before. On the morning of presentation, he was more confused than usual, and then she found him on the floor seizing. He had been compliant with rifaximin and lactulose. He is 1 year sober. His levetiracetam had been recently increased from 500 mg BID to 1000 mg BID by his neurologist 3 weeks ago — girlfriend reports he may have missed some doses in the past week ('he kept forgetting'). On arrival he remains unresponsive with a GCS of 9.

neurological_exam.additional: GCS 9 after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Tongue laceration. Urinary incontinence during the episode. Bilateral extensor plantar responses.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 4 mm, equal, sluggishly reactive. Doll's eye reflex intact. No nystagmus.
neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 9 (E2V3M4). Minimally responsive. Does not follow commands. Eye opening to pain. Incomprehensible sounds. Purposeful withdrawal to pain. Asterixis cannot be assessed at this level of consciousness. Girlfriend reports the convulsion about 30 minutes before EMS arrival.
neurological_exam.motor: Minimal spontaneous movement. Purposeful withdrawal pain.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTRs 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses extensor (Babinski) bilaterally.
